findings.title: A P-periodic centre from time 0 is refuted by a finite sideways constraint check at width <= 21, for every P <= 10
findings.claim: Rule 30 is left-permutive, so col0 and col1 force the entire left half-plane. Adding the single-seed light-cone void (cell(t,-m)=0 for t<m) and black left edge (cell(m,-m)=1) gives a system whose obligations grow quadratically in the width read while its freedom grows linearly. Exhaustively: for every P in 1..10 and every P-periodic word, the system is unsatisfiable at some width N <= 21.
findings.scope: Single black cell. Centre periodic FROM TIME 0, no transient. Exhaustive DFS over col1, widths 4..22, periods 1..10. Strictly weaker than Problem 1, which permits a transient.
findings.result: Widest surviving width by period: P=1:0, 2:0, 3:5, 4:8, 5:6, 6:7, 7:15, 8:12, 9:19, 10:21. The longest survivors imitate the real orbit (at P=4 the word 1101; the true centre begins 1101110011000101). CONTROL: the identical checker on the ACTUAL col0/col1 prefixes survives every width 4..199, so it does not reject the truth.

verification.scope: Exhaustive, no sampling. Widths <= 22, periods <= 10, single seed, zero transient. Python 3 stdlib.

limitations: Zero transient. Problem 1 allows any transient and F002 shows two bits defeat the method.
findings.next_action: None as a proof route; F002 closes it. Kept because the no-transient case is cheap to certify and the real-orbit control is reusable.

findings.title: Two bits of transient defeat the finite check, shown by its failure on a case the kit already settles
findings.claim: With col0 free for t<T and P-periodic after, the widest surviving width jumps to the search cap at T=2 for every period tested. The method cannot reach Problem 1.
findings.scope: T in 0..8, P in 1..4, widths to 20; then P=1, T=2 pushed to widths 24 and 28.
findings.result: T=0 and T=1 still die (P=2 at width 4, P=4 at 14). From T=2 onward every period survives to the cap. Decisively: period 1 WITH a transient is proved impossible by Rule30FiniteConfigs.no_column_eventually_constant (Condrey 2026), yet transient 11 with period word 0 (centre 1,1,0,0,0,...) survives widths 24 and 28 with no sign of dying. The check is blunter than a theorem the library already owns.

verification.scope: Exhaustive over transients, patterns and col1 within the stated caps.

limitations: Shows the method is too weak at reachable widths, not that no width works. A better encoding (SAT or BDD rather than exhaustive DFS) could reach further.
findings.next_action: Any successor finite check should first refute (transient 11, period word 0) — a known-false case — before being trusted on an open one. That cheap yardstick is the durable output of this exercise.

findings.title: Defect density does not contract leftward: flat at one half at every depth and every period
findings.claim: Under the Problem 1 negation the depth-1 defect transfer is a pure mask, so the depth-1 defect set can only shrink, while the light cone forces defects arbitrarily far left. If shrinkage continued at every depth the two would collide and Problem 1 would follow.
findings.scope: Real rule 30 orbit, columns 0 to -64, nine periods, t < 2400; rules 90, 150 and 210 as controls where the centre really is eventually periodic.
findings.result: Rule 30 density is flat at 0.50 at every depth and every period: the depth-2 XOR replenishes exactly what the depth-1 mask removes, so there is no contraction to exploit. A second idea died in the same table: rules 90 and 210 show density 0.000-0.018, which looked like a periodic-centre discriminator, but rule 150 has a constant-black centre and density 0.667, so a periodic centre does not imply a sparse defect field.

verification.scope: Descriptive measurement on real orbits. The rule 30 rows do not test the conditional, whose hypothesis is false there.

limitations: Density is a coarse statistic; a weighted or positional measure could contract where the raw density does not.
findings.next_action: Drop the contraction framing. If revisited, measure a weighted resource and test it on rule 150, where the hypothesis genuinely holds.
